chunks.text: In 1919, a giant wave crashed through a Boston neighborhood. But it wasn't water. It was molasses.
On January 15th, just after lunch, a fifty-foot steel tank by the harbor burst open.
About two point three million gallons of thick, sticky syrup poured into the streets.
The wave was up to twenty-five feet tall, and moved about thirty-five miles an hour.
It smashed buildings and bent the steel tracks of the elevated train.
Twenty-one people died, and about a hundred and fifty were hurt.
Then came the cold. As night fell, the molasses got even thicker, trapping people and slowing rescuers.
And the tank? Neighbors had seen it leaking. The company's fix was to paint it brown, so the drips wouldn't show.
After years in court, the owners were found responsible.
The disaster helped bring stricter building rules across the country.
For decades, people said that on hot days, the neighborhood still smelled sweet.
Today the spot is a park with a small plaque. Follow for more weird history.
